newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union boss urges 35-hour week for all.
newsitem.headline: German union boss urges 35-hour week for all.

text.p: Klaus Zwickel, head of the metal and engineering union IG Metall said on Wednesday a 35-hour week should be implemented in all industry sectors in a bid to halve Germany's unemployment by the year 2000.
For his own sector, Zwickel proposed a shift to a 32-hour week, with some employees working only four days.

"Together with the reduction in overtime and the increase in part-time work a 35-hour working week must be put through in all industry sectors," Zwickel said on the second day of a union-organised jobs conference in Berlin.

Zwickel said that by the end of 1998 a 35-hour working week would be written into contracts across the west German metal sector. IG Metall would then "concentrate on the implementation of a general 32-hour week and four-day weeks for individual workers", he added.

IG Metall pushed through the move to a 35-hour working week amid great triumph in the early 1990's, negotiating that wages should remain unchanged despite the smaller number of hours worked by the individual employee.
Zwickel conceded however that this time around full maintenance of wage levels could not accompany such a shortened working week.
"(But) a complete proportional drop in wages is also scacely acceptable," he said.
IG Metall would be willing to discuss various ways in which wages could be reduced according to individual income groups or according to accompanying job creation measures, Zwickel said.
He added that, in any case, the Federal Labour Office could be involved in making a financial contribution to such schemes as a result of the drop in joblessness that could be expected to follow.
